compiled.subject: architecture
compiled.definition: A status bit set by many processors when an addition carries out of the top bit. On x86 it is also set when a subtraction borrows; ARM uses the opposite sense for subtraction (carry set means no borrow). After an addition it signals unsigned overflow.
compiled.example: Adding 0xFF + 0x01 in 8 bits gives 0x00 with the carry flag set.

reviews.intendedDefinition: A status flag whose meaning depends on the instruction and architecture. After flag-setting addition it reports unsigned carry out; after subtraction Arm reports no borrow while x86 CF reports borrow. Some shifts and other instructions use or preserve it differently.
reviews.intendedMeaning: Unsigned carry out after flag-setting addition; subtraction polarity depends on ISA; instructions can preserve the flag or use it differently.
reviews.rationale: The x86 borrow versus Arm no-borrow distinction is correct. However, the unqualified final sentence and example omit the flag-setting requirement, which was part of the reviewed correction. An Arm addition that does not set flags can leave C from an earlier instruction, so C need not describe the latest addition. The same-ID compiled text therefore does not fully convey the intended instruction-dependent scope.

ownerDependency.requiredChange: Qualify addition and subtraction statements as applying to instructions that update the flag, and qualify the example as a flag-setting addition. Preserve the correct x86/Arm borrow distinction. A sentence stating that other instructions may preserve the flag or use it differently would fully retain the reviewed scope.
ownerDependency.suggestedDefinition: A status flag whose meaning depends on the instruction and architecture. After flag-setting addition it reports unsigned carry out; after flag-setting subtraction x86 CF reports borrow while Arm C reports no borrow. Other instructions may preserve the flag or use it differently.
ownerDependency.suggestedExample: For a flag-setting 8-bit addition, 0xFF + 0x01 gives 0x00 with the carry flag set.

compiledSourceEntry.definition: A status bit set by many processors when an addition carries out of the top bit. On x86 it is also set when a subtraction borrows; ARM uses the opposite sense for subtraction (carry set means no borrow). After an addition it signals unsigned overflow.
compiledSourceEntry.example: Adding 0xFF + 0x01 in 8 bits gives 0x00 with the carry flag set.

compiled.subject: architecture
compiled.definition: A processor status bit reporting that a signed result is not representable at the instruction's width. For two's-complement addition, this happens when same-sign operands produce an opposite-sign retained result; subtraction has a different sign test, and only relevant flag-setting instructions update the flag.
compiled.example: 100 + 100 in 8 bits gives 1100 1000 with the overflow flag set.

reviews.intendedDefinition: A status flag reporting that an arithmetic result does not fit the signed two's-complement range. For the fixed-width binary addition and subtraction circuits taught here, it is the XOR of the carries entering and leaving the sign bit; other operations follow their ISA's flag rules.
reviews.intendedMeaning: Signed overflow at a fixed instruction width; addition and subtraction use their own sign rules; the carry-XOR circuit identity is restricted to the fixed-width add/sub circuits, and flags follow per-instruction ISA rules.
reviews.rationale: The compiled text explicitly limits the same-sign test to two's-complement addition, distinguishes subtraction, names the instruction width, and says only relevant flag-setting instructions update the flag. This preserves the intended conceptual meaning. It omits the carry-XOR implementation identity rather than contradicting or overgeneralising it; that identity remains explicitly scoped in the reviewed lesson.
